basis: New mission, no workbook source. Researched via WebSearch (Sep 2026). Key facts: Taiwan's overall food self-sufficiency rate (calorie basis) was 30.3% in 2023 (18-year low) and 30.7% in 2024 (Ministry of Agriculture / Agriculture and Food Agency 糧食供需年報, via Focus Taiwan, Taipei Times, 上下游新聞); grain self-sufficiency 25.5% in 2023 vs 26.6% in 2022; rice self-sufficiency near 100% (97.7% in 2023, 24万公頃/~1.21M tonnes/yr); wheat ~0.3%, soybean <1%, feed corn ~2.5% self-sufficient, ~8M tonnes coarse grain imported yearly (SETN, 農傳媒); legal rice reserve minimum 3 months/25% of consumption since 2006, above FAO's 17-18% and Japan/Korea targets, actual stock ~1.06M tonnes (~11 months) per Dec 2025 CNA report; WTO rice import TRQ of 144,720 tonnes/year since 2002 accession; 大糧倉計畫 (Grand Grain Silo plan) since 2016 paying farmers to convert paddies to soybean/feed corn, expanded 2022; Typhoon Krathon Oct 2024 vegetable wholesale price NT$63.7/kg then -17% to NT$52.8/kg (Taiwan News); 2023 rice harvest hurt by irrigation suspension, Typhoon Koinu, winter monsoon. Level is carried by syntax and lexical load per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md, not by word count.

slides.1: A typhoon can strip supermarket shelves completely bare within hours, with prices typically spiking for a few days before supply gradually stabilises. What happens, though, in the year that disruption simply refuses to resolve itself?
slides.2: SDG 2 extends well beyond alleviating hunger in distant countries. It's fundamentally concerned with food security, meaning genuinely reliable daily access to enough food, a standard that applies to Taiwan as much as anywhere else.
slides.3: Taiwan, a densely populated island of roughly 23 million residents, imports the majority of what it consumes by sea. In 2024, only 30.7 percent of domestic food consumption was actually produced here.
slides.4: That figure has been declining for years, rather than improving as officials once hoped. It fell to an eighteen-year low of 30.3 percent in 2023, recovering only marginally since that particular low point.
slides.5: Breaking the numbers apart reveals a much sharper picture. Rice approaches near-total self-sufficiency, whereas overall grain self-sufficiency sits at merely 25.5 percent, given that wheat is almost entirely imported from abroad.
slides.6: So the rice occupying your plate was almost certainly cultivated domestically. The bread accompanying it, however, certainly wasn't, nor was the cooking oil in which it happened to be fried.
slides.7: Cultivated across roughly 240,000 hectares in two annual harvests, rice remains genuinely secure here. About 1.21 million tonnes are produced every year, keeping this staple reliably available for everyone.
slides.8: Legislative protection has also been established for this staple. A mandatory reserve, equal to three months of national consumption, is required by law to exceed Japan's own comparable target clearly.
slides.9: Since 2016, the Grand Grain Silo initiative has compensated farmers for converting rice paddies into soybean fields instead. This has gradually eroded decades of entrenched import dependency in the process.
slides.10: Rather than leaving idle paddies unproductive, farmers can now contract to cultivate feed corn there instead. This effectively converts otherwise wasted land into a modest yet genuine source of domestic grain.
slides.11: Researchers here have also begun trialling feed rice as a possible substitute for imported feed grain, for pig farms too. This work could gradually reduce reliance on any single imported commodity.
slides.12: This is still not a free achievement, though. A tonne of soybean cultivated domestically is priced much higher than one imported from abroad, so somebody inevitably still absorbs that difference.
slides.13: Sourcing grain from whichever market proves cheapest works well enough in an ordinary, uneventful year. That's exactly why our heavy dependence on imports goes largely unexamined by the general public.
slides.14: Global trade regulations, however, are not adjusted to reflect domestic circumstances. Taiwan has been obligated since 2002 to import a fixed quota of rice annually, regardless of how full domestic reserves already are.
slides.15: The margin proves considerably thinner than it first appears. Facing Typhoon Krathon in 2024, Taipei's wholesale vegetable price spiked sharply, only gradually easing once the storm had eventually passed through.
slides.16: What this arrangement reveals is a system engineered for efficiency rather than resilience. It quietly sustains low everyday prices while leaving minimal slack for the year two disruptions coincide unexpectedly.
slides.17: In summary, Taiwan simultaneously holds two quite contradictory numbers at the same time. It approaches total self-sufficiency in rice alone, yet reaches only around 30 percent self-sufficiency across the entire food supply overall.
slides.18: This trade-off is one your generation stands to inherit directly. It is agronomists and engineers, quite possibly some of you, who will ultimately decide how much self-sufficiency is worth paying for.
slides.19: So here is a concrete request worth seriously considering right now. Pay closer attention to where your food is actually sourced, and track agricultural policy as it surfaces within the news.
slides.20: Current abundance, however, offers no guarantee whatsoever regarding future supply. Rather than passively waiting for an actual crisis to strike, these difficult questions deserve to be raised well in advance.
